Fit a Bayesian Gaussian-process regression with brms

Source: R/model-bayesian.R
fit_bayesian_spatial_model.Rd

Fits a regression whose residual spatial structure is modelled as a Gaussian process over the coordinates, and so kept out of the errors. Every quantity has a posterior, so predictions come with intervals; cv_bayes() reports their held-out coverage and CRPS. The spatial term is a smooth surface at a stated resolution. The Gaussian process is fitted through a reduced-rank basis, and that basis has a floor: an effective range below which it cannot represent structure, reported in CRS units as $info$gp_resolution and by print(). With the defaults the floor is about 32 km along each axis on points spread evenly over a 100 km square. Structure shorter than the floor is counted as noise: the fitted range comes out too long, the residual standard deviation too large, and the intervals too narrow where the structure is. See "What the basis resolves" below.

Usage

fit_bayesian_spatial_model(
  data_sf,
  response_var,
  predictor_vars,
  family = NULL,
  gp_k = NULL,
  gp_c = NULL,
  gp_iso = FALSE,
  prior = NULL,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = floor(iter/2),
  cores = getOption("mc.cores", 1L),
  seed = 123,
  backend = c("auto", "cmdstanr", "rstan"),
  control = list(),
  compute_loo = TRUE,
  standardize_predictors = FALSE,
  check_convergence = TRUE,
  pointize = "auto",
  boundary = NULL,
  gp_resolution = NULL,
  .already_prepped = FALSE
)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf object with response, predictors, and geometries.

response_var

Response column name.

predictor_vars

Predictor column names. May be character(0) for an intercept-only model: the response is then explained by the intercept and the spatial Gaussian process alone, the baseline for asking how much of the surface is spatial structure and how much covariate effect, and the null model to compare a covariate model with in compare_models().

family

A model family accepted by brms::brm(): a stats family function such as poisson(), or a brms family object such as brms::zero_inflated_poisson(), brms::negbinomial(), brms::hurdle_poisson(), brms::bernoulli() or brms::Beta(). Default NULL, resolved to stats::gaussian(). The family reaches brms::brm() unchanged with the spatial GP term still in the formula. A factor response is accepted only under brms::categorical() or an ordinal family, and those fits have no single expected value per row, so several methods cannot use them; see "Non-Gaussian responses" for what each family supports, and the count example below.

gp_k

Positive integer giving the number of GP basis functions per dimension, or NULL (default) to derive it from the length-scale/domain ratio. The fitted model carries gp_k^2 basis functions, not gp_k (see "GP basis count and boundary factor"). A value above the derived one makes the basis finer, and the length-scale prior's lower tail moves down to the length-scale that basis resolves, because a finer basis under the default prior gains almost nothing. A value below the derived one leaves the prior where it was, mostly below what the basis resolves; that share is stored as $info$gp_adequacy$prior_mass_below, logged when it passes 10 percent and flagged by print(). To ask for a resolution in CRS units, use gp_resolution and leave this NULL.

gp_c

Positive numeric boundary factor for the approximate GP, or NULL (default) to derive it alongside gp_k. The boundary must be wide enough to contain the longest plausible effective range; a value that is too small truncates the domain and degrades the approximation for smooth, long-range surfaces. When you set gp_c and leave gp_k = NULL, gp_k is derived for your boundary: a wider boundary needs more basis functions to resolve the same length-scale, so raising gp_c raises the derived gp_k with it, up to the cap of 50 per dimension (a capped value is logged).

gp_iso

Logical; passed to brms::gp(iso = ). FALSE (the default) fits a separate length-scale per coordinate axis, so the model learns any directional structure from the data. TRUE fits a single length-scale shared by both standardised axes, which makes the kernel anisotropic in the original CRS by the ratio sd(X)/sd(Y), because the coordinates are standardised per axis beforehand. See "Coordinate scaling and anisotropy".

prior

Optional brms prior specification. When NULL and standardize_predictors = TRUE, a weakly informative prior is set on the regression coefficients, on the scale of the linear predictor: normal(0, 2.5 * sd(y)) under an identity link (gaussian, student, skew-normal and mixtures of them), normal(0, 2.5 * sd(log(y))) for the lognormal families, whose location is on the log scale, and the fixed normal(0, 5) under any other link (log, logit and so on), where the linear predictor has a scale of its own. sd() is taken over the training rows. The result therefore does not depend on the units of the response. The prior brms used is stored as $info$b_prior and shown by print(). When prior is given, no slope prior is added. A prior given here on a class that lives on the response's scale (b, Intercept, sigma, sdgp, and beta of exgaussian()) keeps the response as it is; see "The response's centre and scale". A GP length-scale prior set from the data is added unless prior already contains an entry with class = "lscale".

chains

Number of MCMC chains. Default 4.

iter

Total iterations per chain. Default 2000.

warmup

Warmup iterations. Default floor(iter / 2).

cores

Number of cores for the sampler, one chain per core. Default getOption("mc.cores", 1L), the convention brms uses itself, so options(mc.cores = 4) once per session runs the four default chains in parallel everywhere.

seed

Integer seed. Default 123.

backend

"auto" (default), "cmdstanr" or "rstan". "auto" uses cmdstanr only when a CmdStan build is available, and rstan otherwise, which brms always brings. The cmdstanr package is a thin interface and can be installed without a CmdStan build (cmdstanr::install_cmdstan() builds one). An explicit "cmdstanr" with no usable CmdStan raises an error that says how to install it, before the sampler starts.

control

Named list of sampler controls, merged over the package defaults list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 12) rather than replacing them, so list(max_treedepth = 15) keeps adapt_delta = 0.99. See "Sampler settings".

compute_loo

Logical; compute PSIS-LOO. Default TRUE.

standardize_predictors

Logical; centre and scale numeric predictors before fitting. Default FALSE. When TRUE, the centre and scale of each predictor are stored in $info$predictor_scaling and applied again by predict(). The model is then fitted on the standardised predictors, so coef() reports a slope per standard deviation of each predictor and an intercept at the predictor means, not the raw-unit values stats::lm() would give (see spatial_fit-coef).

check_convergence

Logical, default TRUE. After fitting, read the sampler's diagnostics and the GP basis against the posterior and the residuals, and set $info$convergence_ok and $info$gp_adequacy. See "Convergence checks" and "What the basis resolves". FALSE skips both, leaves convergence_ok NA (not checked) and sets the adequacy status to "not_checked".

pointize

How a feature that is not a point is reduced to one: one of "auto" (default), "centroid", "point_on_surface", "surface", "line_midpoint" or "bbox_center"; see coerce_to_points().

boundary

Optional polygonal sf/sfc whose CRS the data are projected to. It is not a clip: rows outside it are kept.

gp_resolution

The shortest effective range the basis should resolve, as a single positive number in the units of the data's CRS (metres for a UTM layer), or NULL (default) for the rule described under "GP basis count and boundary factor". gp_k is derived from it, and the length-scale prior's lower tail moves with the basis. It can only refine: a value the default basis already resolves leaves the default basis in place. It is an error when the basis it needs exceeds the cap of 50 functions per dimension (2,500 in all); the message gives the basis size needed and the shortest range the cap reaches on this layout. Cost grows with gp_k^2. Give gp_resolution or gp_k, not both.

.already_prepped

Internal; leave at the default.

Value

A bayesian_fit object (inherits from spatial_fit). Supports predict(), fitted(), residuals(), coef(), summary(), and model_metrics(). Model-specific metadata lives in $info (coords: the names of the scaled coordinate columns handed to brms::gp(); coord_scaling, predictor_scaling, gp_k, gp_c, gp_iso, gp_n_basis, gp_ell_min, gp_resolution: the smallest effective range the basis resolves, as c(x, y) in CRS units; gp_resolution_requested: the gp_resolution argument, or NULL; gp_prefit: the check made before sampling, a list with status ("ok"; "below_floor", the one that warns; "below_floor_no_autocorrelation" and "below_floor_long_range", a range below the floor that the short-lag or the floor-distance test did not bear out; "not_estimated" or "not_run"), range (the estimated range in CRS units), floor, k_needed, moran and moran_floor (the two Moran's I tests, each with I, z and a one-sided p; NULL where the test is not run, or where the residuals are the rounding of an exact fit), reason and unit; gp_adequacy: a list with status (see "What the basis resolves"), frac_below (the share of length-scale draws below gp_ell_min), identified and identified_by ("spatial_share" or "length_scale", the rule that decided it; see "What the basis resolves"), contraction (one minus the ratio of posterior to prior variance, per length-scale, negative when the posterior is the wider of the two) and prior_gap (the largest gap between the posterior's and the prior's distribution functions, per length-scale; both NA for a length-scale prior this function did not set), spatial_share and sdgp (2.5, 50 and 97.5 percent quantiles; the share only for a gaussian or lognormal family), effective_range (the posterior effective range per axis in CRS units, same quantiles), residual_moran (the test on the residuals the status rests on: I, z, a one-sided p and k, the number of neighbours; absent when it could not be run, and residual_untested then says why), resolution, unit and prior_mass_below; b_prior: the slope prior brms used ("(flat)" for its default, NA for a model with no slopes), and b_prior_source: where it came from; predictor_levels: the levels each factor or character predictor has in the training rows, which predict() holds new data to; gp_S: the pooled centred range brms::gp(c = ) multiplies; gp_cmeans: the column means brms centred the scaled coordinates on; gp_xy_range: the training extrema of the scaled coordinates, which predict() uses, with gp_S and gp_cmeans, to hold the GP boundary at its fitted value; gp_lengthscale_bounds: the c(lower, upper) the length-scale prior was calibrated over; gp_lscale_prior: the length-scale prior brms::validate_prior() reports the model will actually use, which is not necessarily the one this function requested (several entries, semicolon-separated, if brms resolved the axes differently); loo, looic, convergence_ok (TRUE or FALSE, and NA when nothing was checked, as under check_convergence = FALSE), convergence_diagnostics: n_divergent, n_max_treedepth, ebfmi (per chain), max_rhat, min_neff_ratio, min_ess (the smallest bulk or tail effective sample size) and ess_required (100 per chain), and rhat_failed / neff_failed / ess_failed, the parameters that failed each check by name with their values (R-hat, ESS ratio and ESS; empty when none failed), which is what makes a failed check actionable, rhat_caution, the parameters whose R-hat is between 1.01 and 1.05 with enough effective draws, which do not fail the verdict, plus gp_lscale_below_resolution and gp_adequacy, the share and status described under "What the basis resolves"; and n_dropped: the rows prep_model_data() removed for missing or non-finite values or a bad geometry, so $n can be read against nrow(data_sf)); response_scaling: the centre and scale the response was handed to brms with, absent when it was handed over as it is (see "The response's centre and scale"). The raw brmsfit is in $engine.

Details

The fitted length-scale is an estimate of how far the spatial dependence reaches only when its posterior sits clear of both that floor and its prior. $info$gp_adequacy says whether it does, and when it does $info$gp_adequacy$effective_range holds the posterior effective range per axis in CRS units (the raw lscale draws are in per-axis standardised units and are not a distance).

Choose it over fit_gwr_model() when you want one global relationship plus a spatial random field, with posterior intervals; choose GWR when the question is how a coefficient varies across the map. Choose fit_rf_model() when predictive accuracy matters more than an interpretable model and the response is non-linear in the predictors. The cost is time: this is full MCMC through brms and Stan, so a fit takes minutes rather than seconds, and the basis size (gp_k) trades fidelity against run time.

Sampler settings

adapt_delta defaults to 0.99, not Stan's 0.8, because one divergent transition sets convergence_ok to FALSE (see "Convergence checks") and lower values can leave a few on ordinary data. A lower value, such as list(adapt_delta = 0.9), runs faster, since the smaller step of 0.99 costs sampling time. Some divergent transitions can remain at 0.99 too, for example on a layer whose spatial field is weak against the noise; then raise it to 0.995 or 0.999, which costs more time again.

Convergence checks

Under check_convergence = TRUE the verdict in $info$convergence_ok follows Stan's own diagnostics, with these thresholds:

  • any divergent transition after warmup;

  • bulk or tail effective sample size below 100 per chain for any parameter (Vehtari et al. 2021; the rule rstan warns on). It is an absolute count, not a share of the draws;

  • rank-normalised split R-hat, in two tiers. Above 1.05, the value rstan's own sampler warning uses, for any parameter. Above 1.01, the value Vehtari et al. (2021) recommend, for a parameter whose effective sample size is also below the count in the previous item, or cannot be read;

  • E-BFMI below 0.3 in any chain (Betancourt 2016).

An R-hat between 1.01 and 1.05 on a parameter with enough effective draws is a caution, not a failure: it is stored by name in $info$convergence_diagnostics$rhat_caution, logged, and counted by print(). The model has one weight per basis function, about 540 parameters at the basis derived for points spread evenly over a square, and among that many the largest R-hat sits near 1.01 in a fit that has converged. Vehtari et al. give 1.01 beside an effective sample size above 400, so the two are read together here.

Transitions that stop at max_treedepth are counted and logged but do not change the verdict: Stan treats them as a cost, not as invalid draws. A failed verdict sets convergence_ok to FALSE, raises one R warning of class spatialkit_convergence naming each failed check with its count and its first five parameters, and print() flags it; $info$convergence_diagnostics holds every value. The warning closes with the remedy for the checks that failed: a higher adapt_delta for divergent transitions, which more iterations do not remove, and more iterations for R-hat and effective sample size. A short run usually fails on effective sample size. cv_bayes() marks such folds in fold_metrics$convergence_ok and compare_models() names such a model.

The same step checks the GP basis against the posterior and the residuals (see "What the basis resolves") and stores the result as $info$gp_adequacy. The residuals need the fitted values, one pass over the posterior that fitted() caches for later calls. That check is about the approximation, not the sampler, so it does not change convergence_ok; print() and summary() show its status, and two of its states raise a warning of class spatialkit_gp_adequacy.

GP basis count and boundary factor

brms::gp() builds a full tensor grid over its covariates, so a term gp(..x, ..y, k = gp_k) carries gp_k^2 basis functions: the gp_k argument is the count per dimension, not the total rank. Both gp_k and gp_c are therefore chosen from the ratio of the estimated length-scale to the domain extent, following Riutort-Mayol et al. (2023): gp_c is set large enough to contain the upper length-scale bound, and gp_k large enough to resolve the lower one. The derived value depends on the layout, not on n: about 23 for points spread evenly over a square; other layouts give other values, up to the cap of 50.

The domain extent used is the one brms::gp(c = ) itself multiplies: the full pooled range of the column-centred coordinates (brms:::choose_L(), taken over the unique coordinate rows, because brms:::.data_gp() reduces the covariates to unique rows first under the default gr = TRUE, so repeat visits to one location do not widen the domain), not the per-axis half-range in which Riutort-Mayol et al. state their inequalities. Both constraints are on the boundary \(L = c \times S\), and stating them in brms's units keeps gp_c, gp_k and $info$gp_ell_min describing the basis brms builds. A gp_c derived on the half-range convention and handed to brms::gp() produces a boundary twice as wide as intended, against which gp_k under-resolves by a factor of two.

The GP term is built with scale = FALSE. brms::gp() otherwise rescales its covariates so the maximum Euclidean distance between two points is 1, and reports lscale in that space; since this function already standardises the coordinates, and the length-scale prior, gp_c and the adequacy check below are all expressed in those standardised units, a second normalisation would leave every length-scale quantity in the wrong units.

What the basis resolves

The smallest length-scale the chosen basis can resolve is 1.75 * gp_c * S / gp_k, stored in standardised units as $info$gp_ell_min. As an effective range (the distance at which the squared-exponential correlation has fallen to 5 percent, 2.45 length-scales) and in CRS units it is $info$gp_resolution, one value per axis because each coordinate is divided by its own standard deviation. The floor is soft: the basis keeps 99 percent of a process's variance at the floor, 69 percent at half of it and 41 percent at a third. The default length-scale prior is what makes it bind, with 1 percent of its mass below the floor and about one part in a hundred million below half of it.

Three checks hold the basis against the data.

  1. Before anything is compiled, the autocorrelation range of the response (of its OLS residuals when there are predictors) is estimated with estimate_sac_range() and compared with the coarser axis's floor. That range is a variogram estimate and can be wrong in both directions, so a range below the floor raises a warning only when two other things agree with it. The same variable is autocorrelated at short range (Moran's I over 4 nearest neighbours, one-sided, at 5 percent): a variogram fitted to a response with no spatial structure can still return a short range, though estimate_sac_range() refuses most such layers itself. And it is no longer autocorrelated at the floor's distance (Moran's I over the pairs 0.75 to 1.25 floors apart is not both above 0.05, the correlation that defines an effective range, and significant at 5 percent): a variogram can also return a short range for a surface that is smooth over long distances. The warning has class spatialkit_gp_resolution, gives both numbers and the basis size that would resolve the range, says that it is an estimate which the check after sampling tests against the residuals of the fitted model, and says when the basis size is past the cap or past the number of rows, where kriging is the better tool if the range is right. A short range the floor-distance test contradicts is logged and shown by print() without a warning: it can still mean short-range structure beside a longer one, which the basis counts as noise. Nothing before sampling separates the two; the residuals after it do (the third check). A range that cannot be estimated is logged with the reason and shown by print(); the result is in $info$gp_prefit. An exponential field has structure at every scale, so the warning on one is not plainly wrong.

  2. Also before sampling, the share of the length-scale prior below the floor is computed ($info$gp_adequacy$prior_mass_below). A derived basis keeps it near 0.01; a small gp_k does not, and a share above 0.10 is logged and flagged by print().

  3. After sampling, under check_convergence = TRUE, the posterior and the residuals are read. The posterior says whether the Gaussian process carries a share of the variance and where its length-scale sits against the floor. It cannot say what the surface left behind, so the residuals are tested for autocorrelation at short range in every fit (Moran's I over 4 nearest neighbours, one-sided, at 5 percent; $info$gp_adequacy$residual_moran). $info$gp_adequacy$status is one of:

    "ok"

    The Gaussian process carries a share of the variance, its length-scale is clear of the floor, and the residuals show no autocorrelation at short range. A surface smoother than the prior expects (a plane, a range longer than the extent) is "ok": its length-scale posterior sits on the long side of the prior and is wider than it.

    "below_resolution"

    The Gaussian process carries a share of the variance and more than 10 percent of the length-scale draws fall below the floor. The 10 percent trigger is this package's operationalisation of the check Riutort-Mayol et al. recommend, not a figure from the paper.

    "unresolved_short_range"

    The residuals are autocorrelated at short range: the signature of structure finer than the basis, counted as noise. It is reached two ways, and $info$gp_adequacy$identified says which. The Gaussian process carries no variance that can be told from zero (FALSE): all of the structure is below the floor. Or it carries a share and its length-scale is clear of the floor (TRUE): it fitted a surface, and finer structure sits beside it, as with a regional trend plus short-range structure.

    "no_signal_above_floor"

    The Gaussian process carries no variance that can be told from zero, and the residuals show nothing left over. A response with no spatial structure gives this, so it is not a failure by itself.

    "not_checked"

    check_convergence = FALSE.

    The second and third raise a warning of class spatialkit_gp_adequacy; the fourth is logged. When the residuals cannot be tested (an ordinal or categorical family has no residual per row; a posterior that cannot be drawn), the status rests on the posterior alone, a line is logged, the reason is in $info$gp_adequacy$residual_untested, and print() keeps its flag on a variogram range that was below the floor.

    On a fit with nothing left over the test is conservative, because the surface takes up part of the noise and leaves the residuals slightly negatively autocorrelated. It is not sharp just below the floor, where the length-scale draws report the structure ("below_resolution"). An exponential field has structure at every scale and can be reported with a range above the floor. The 5 percent level is the usual one and is not tuned; with many rows a small leftover autocorrelation is significant, so read the size of I beside its p.

    "No variance that can be told from zero" is decided on the Gaussian process's share of the variance, sdgp^2 / (sdgp^2 + sigma^2): its 2.5 percent quantile is under 0.01. It does not mark off a response whose structure is all below the floor: such a process can still carry a share, and the residual test reports it. The share exists for a gaussian or lognormal family. For any other family the length-scales decide instead: the process is not identified when on every axis the posterior kept more than three quarters of its prior's variance and the largest gap between its distribution function and the prior's is under 0.30. $info$gp_adequacy$identified_by says which rule was used. The width of the length-scale posterior does not decide by itself, because a posterior that moved to longer length-scales is wider than its prior; and the share of draws below the floor cannot detect an unidentified process, because a posterior the data did not move puts 1 percent below the floor, the same as the prior.

A response whose range is below the floor needs a finer basis and a prior that allows the shorter length-scale, both of which gp_resolution sets, up to the cap. Past the cap this model cannot resolve the range, and kriging, which has no such floor, is the better tool; see kriging_adequacy() for cell means.

Coordinate scaling and anisotropy

Before fitting the GP, X and Y coordinates are each centred and divided by their own standard deviation. This is a conditioning step: easting and northing frequently span very different ranges in a projected CRS, and handing Stan raw metres samples poorly.

Because the axes are scaled independently, a single shared length-scale in the scaled space corresponds to an anisotropic kernel in the original CRS, stretched by the ratio sd(X)/sd(Y). That ratio is a property of how the sampling locations are laid out, not of the process being modelled.

gp_iso = FALSE (the default) therefore fits one length-scale per axis, letting the model estimate directional structure from the data instead of inheriting it from the standardisation. Set gp_iso = TRUE for one length-scale shared by both standardised axes.

gp_iso does not affect cost: brms::gp() builds a tensor grid either way, so the model carries gp_k^2 basis functions regardless. The stored $info$coord_scaling list records the scaling strategy, and $info$gp_iso records which kernel was used.

Warnings

Every warning this function raises carries a condition class, so a caller can catch or muffle exactly one of them by name:

spatialkit_rows_dropped, spatialkit_constant_predictor

From prep_model_data(): incomplete rows were dropped, with the counts; a predictor takes one value in every row kept.

spatialkit_response_scale

The response lies far from zero or its standard deviation far from 1, and prior sets a prior on a class on the response's scale, so the response is handed to brms as it is; see "The response's centre and scale".

spatialkit_gp_basis_size

Fewer than one row per ten basis functions.

spatialkit_gp_resolution

A variogram fitted before compiling puts the response's range below what the basis resolves, and the autocorrelation of the response agrees. An estimate; the check after sampling tests it against the residuals of the fitted model.

spatialkit_convergence

The sampler's diagnostics fail.

spatialkit_gp_adequacy

The basis is too coarse for the data: the posterior asks for a shorter length-scale than it resolves ("below_resolution"), or the residuals are autocorrelated at short range ("unresolved_short_range").

A response that takes a single value is an error, raised before anything is compiled, and so is one whose values differ only by rounding (1e15 and the next double). A fit that comes back from brms with no posterior draws, as when Stan rejects every starting value, is an error that names the response's size as brms was given it. The convergence warning carries the checks that failed as failed ("divergent", "ebfmi", "rhat", "ess"). cv_bayes() fits once per fold; it collects the last four classes from its folds and raises each once for the run, naming the folds, and cv_spatial() does the same for a fit_fn that calls this function.

The response's centre and scale

Stan starts every parameter between -2 and 2, and brms sets its default priors for the intercept, the residual standard deviation and the Gaussian process's standard deviation from the response it is given, with scales of at least 2.5 in its units. A response at 1e8 plus a spread of 1, or in units of 1e-20, lies far from both, and brms can miss the data by orders of magnitude. So under the gaussian, student, skew_normal, exgaussian and asym_laplace families with an identity link, a response whose centre is more than 1,000 times its spread from zero is handed to brms less that centre, and one whose standard deviation lies outside \(2^{-20}\) to \(2^{20}\) is divided by the power of two nearest that standard deviation. Under exgaussian and asym_laplace the rule is narrower: a centre more than 4 times the spread from zero is taken off, and a standard deviation outside \(2^{-2}\) to \(2^{2}\) is divided out, because brms's default prior on exgaussian's beta and Stan's starting values do not follow the response. Both steps are exact, and the model is the same model of the response: the shift moves the location only, and the scale multiplies the location, sigma and the mean beta of exgaussian's exponential part, and leaves the degrees of freedom of student, the skewness of skew_normal and the quantile of asym_laplace as they are. Every other response, and every response under another family, is handed over as it is.

fitted(), predict() and its draws, residuals(), coef(), $info$loo, $info$looic and $info$gp_adequacy$sdgp are put back in the response's units, and $info$b_prior gives the automatic slope prior in those units. The same data from another origin or in other units then give the same fit, up to Monte Carlo error. The centre and scale are in $info$response_scaling. $engine is the fit of the response brms was given, so brms's own functions on it (brms::fixef(), brms::posterior_epred()) answer on that scale.

A prior given in prior on a class on the response's scale (b, Intercept, sigma, sdgp, and beta of exgaussian) is read by brms on the response it is given. With such a prior the response is handed over as it is, and the warning spatialkit_response_scale says so.

Non-Gaussian responses

Nothing in this function is Gaussian-specific except its default. A numeric count, binary (0/1 or logical) or bounded response passes through to brms under the family you name, with the GP term in the formula and the length-scale prior attached to each distributional parameter's GP.

The response check is family-aware. A factor or character response is accepted only under brms::categorical() or an ordinal family (cumulative, sratio, cratio, acat), and refused under every other family before anything is compiled; under gaussian a logical response is refused too. The case to watch is a two-level factor under brms::bernoulli(): brms would fit it, but residuals(), summary(), model_metrics() and cv_bayes() could not score a factor, so convert it to 0/1 first.

An ordinal or categorical fit has a probability per response category, not one expected value per row. predict() with its default type = "epred", fitted(), residuals(), summary() and model_metrics() therefore stop with a message saying so, and cv_bayes() refuses the family before fitting anything. predict(type = "predict", draws = TRUE) returns the posterior predicted categories, as category indices, for new rows as well as the training ones (the share of draws in each category estimates its probability), and brms::posterior_epred(fit$engine) the probabilities for the training rows.

For the numeric families two things follow. First, the metrics that come back from model_metrics() and the cv_*() functions are not all meaningful for such a response: RMSE and MAE are, MAPE, SMAPE and R-squared are Gaussian-shaped, and for this backend cv_bayes()'s CRPS and interval coverage are the proper scores to read. See model_metrics(), section "Which metrics survive a non-Gaussian response". Second, estimate_sac_range() fits a variogram to the raw response (or OLS residuals), whose variance tracks its mean for a count; the range it reports is then less trustworthy than for a Gaussian response, and its help page says how.

The response check reads the family's name through brms's own accessor. If brms cannot name the family object, the check is skipped, and a wrong response type surfaces as a Stan error with no message from this function.

Spatial confounding

A fixed-effect coefficient estimated alongside a spatial random effect is a different quantity from the same coefficient in a non-spatial fit. When a covariate is itself spatially smooth, the GP term absorbs part of its effect and the two estimates can disagree sharply; when the response is smoother than the covariate, the estimate can shrink toward zero regardless of the true effect (Bolin and Wallin 2026). Under a correctly specified spatial model this is not a bias but a change of estimand (Zimmerman and Ver Hoef 2022): the spatial coefficient is the effect net of whatever the spatial field can explain, and the non-spatial one is not. The right one depends on the question, so report both side by side, unadjusted: fit the same formula with stats::lm() or stats::glm() and compare. Compare like with like: under standardize_predictors = TRUE the coefficients here are per standard deviation of each predictor, so either fit the non-spatial model on the same standardised columns or divide these slopes by $info$predictor_scaling[[name]]$scale first (see spatial_fit-coef).

Published work on remedies is unsettled, and this function takes no side. Restricted spatial regression (Hughes and Haran 2013) projects the spatial effect off the covariate space; later work argues it does not deliver what it promises (Hanks et al. 2015; Khan and Calder 2022). Within this backend, modelling the covariate and the spatial field as explicitly correlated (Marques, Kneib and Klein 2022) is expressible in a brms formula with no new code, and a spectral adjustment (Guan et al. 2023) is the principled route that suits a Hilbert-space basis; this function does not implement it.

See also

cv_bayes() to score the fit on spatial folds; predict() (spatial_fit-predict) and coef() (spatial_fit-coef); gp_lengthscale_bounds() for the length-scale range the prior is set over.

Other model fitting: fit_gwr_model(), fit_rf_model(), gp_lengthscale_bounds(), new_spatial_fit()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Not run: fits with Stan, which needs a working C++ toolchain and takes
# minutes of sampling.
if (requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(sf)
  set.seed(1)
  n <- 60
  dat <- st_as_sf(
    data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
               elev = rnorm(n)),
    coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
  )
  dat$price <- 10 + 0.01 * (st_coordinates(dat)[, 1] - 5e5) +
    2 * dat$elev + rnorm(n)
  # Two short chains keep this to a few minutes; Stan may warn about
  # effective sample size, which is the cost of that.  Use its defaults
  # (chains = 4, iter = 2000) for a fit to report.
  fit <- fit_bayesian_spatial_model(dat, "price", "elev",
                                    chains = 2, iter = 1000,
                                    compute_loo = FALSE)
  print(summary(fit))
  head(predict(fit, newdata = dat))

  # A zero-inflated count.  The family is the only thing that changes.
  # summary()'s R2 and MAPE assume a Gaussian response, so for a count
  # read the coefficients here and score the model with cv_bayes(), whose
  # CRPS and interval coverage are defined for any response.
  dat$count <- rpois(n, exp(0.5 + 0.8 * dat$elev)) * rbinom(n, 1, 0.7)
  fit_zip <- fit_bayesian_spatial_model(dat, "count", "elev",
                                        family = brms::zero_inflated_poisson(),
                                        chains = 2, iter = 1000,
                                        compute_loo = FALSE)
  coef(fit_zip)
}
} # }
